---
title: "The Monty Hall problem: should you switch?"
description: "The famous three-door problem: play it interactively, see why switching wins with probability 2/3 using Bayes' theorem, and what changes when the host does not know where the car is."
date: 2027-01-11
categories: [Probability, Bayes, R, Interactive]
keywords: [Monty Hall problem, three doors, Bayes theorem, conditional probability, probability paradox, simulation, should you switch]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
```

You are on a game show, facing three closed doors, A, B and C. Behind one is a car, behind the other two a goat each. The host knows where the car is. You pick a door, say A. The host opens one of the other two, say B, and shows a goat. Then he asks: **do you keep A or switch to C?**

Most people answer that it does not matter: two doors are left, so 50% each. The correct answer is that **switching wins with probability 2/3**. The problem is named after the host of the American game show *Let's Make a Deal*, and it is perhaps the best-known example that [information changes probabilities](../conditional-probability/index.qmd), as long as we know **how** it was given.

## Play

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Three doors
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const names = ["A", "B", "C"];
  let car, pick, opened, stage;
  const stats = {stay: [0, 0], swit: [0, 0]};
  const root = html`<div></div>`, msg = html`<div class="ix-note" style="min-height:2.6em"></div>`, doorsBox = html`<div style="display:flex;gap:10px;margin:8px 0"></div>`, statBox = html`<div></div>`;
  const newGame = () => { car = Math.floor(3 * Math.random()); pick = null; opened = null; stage = 0; render(); };
  const door = i => {
    const isOpen = opened === i || stage === 2;
    const face = isOpen ? (i === car ? "🚗" : "🐐") : names[i];
    const b = html`<button style="width:4.2em;height:5.5em;font-size:1.4em;margin:0;border-width:2px;${pick === i ? "border-color:#f28e2b;background:#fff4e8" : ""}">${face}</button>`;
    b.disabled = stage === 2 || opened === i;
    b.onclick = () => {
      if (stage === 0) {
        pick = i;
        const goats = [0, 1, 2].filter(j => j !== pick && j !== car);
        opened = goats[Math.floor(Math.random() * goats.length)];
        stage = 1;
      } else if (stage === 1) {
        const switched = i !== pick;
        pick = i; stage = 2;
        const win = pick === car;
        const s = switched ? stats.swit : stats.stay;
        s[0] += win ? 1 : 0; s[1] += 1;
      }
      render();
    };
    return b;
  };
  const render = () => {
    doorsBox.replaceChildren(...[0, 1, 2].map(door));
    if (stage === 0) msg.innerHTML = "Pick a door.";
    else if (stage === 1) msg.innerHTML = `You picked door <b>${names[pick]}</b>. The host opened door <b>${names[opened]}</b>: a goat. Press <b>${names[pick]}</b> again to stay, or the other closed door to switch.`;
    else msg.innerHTML = pick === car ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ You won the car!</span>` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ A goat.</span> The car was behind door <b>${names[car]}</b>.`;
    const r = ([w, n]) => n ? `${w} / ${n} (${(100 * w / n).toFixed(0)}%)` : "–";
    statBox.innerHTML = `<table class="ix-tbl"><tr><th>Strategy</th><th>Wins / games</th></tr>
      <tr><td>Stay</td><td><b>${r(stats.stay)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Switch</td><td><b>${r(stats.swit)}</b></td></tr></table>`;
  };
  const again = html`<button>New game</button>`;
  again.onclick = newGame;
  newGame();
  root.append(doorsBox, msg, again, statBox);
  return root;
}
```
:::

Play 10–20 times with each strategy. With few games the percentages are unstable, but switching soon starts to pull ahead.

## Why 2/3: every case

Suppose the car is behind B. Your first pick is equally likely to be A, B or C:

| First pick | The host opens | If you stay | If you switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | C (forced) | goat | **car** |
| B | A or C | **car** | goat |
| C | A (forced) | goat | **car** |

Switching wins in two of the three equally likely cases. The intuition is simple: your first door hides the car with probability $1/3$, and nothing the host does changes that, since he can **always** open a door with a goat. The remaining $2/3$ "collects" on the only door he left closed.

## With Bayes' theorem

You picked A and the host opened B. Let $C_A$, $C_B$, $C_C$ be the events "the car is behind A, B, C", each with probability $1/3$, and $H$ = {the host opens B}. The likelihoods depend on **how** the host chooses:

- if the car is behind A, he opens B or C at random: $P(H \mid C_A) = 1/2$,
- if it is behind B, he never opens it: $P(H \mid C_B) = 0$,
- if it is behind C, he must open B: $P(H \mid C_C) = 1$.

By [Bayes' theorem](../bayes-theorem/index.qmd):

$$P(C_A \mid H) = \frac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 0 \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{1/6}{1/2} = \frac{1}{3}, \qquad P(C_C \mid H) = \frac{1/3}{1/2} = \frac{2}{3}.$$

## What if the host did not know?

Suppose the host **does not know** where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random. This time it happened to be a goat. Then the likelihoods change: the probability that he opens B **and shows a goat** is $1/2$ if the car is behind A, $0$ if it is behind B and $1/2$ if it is behind C. Bayes gives

$$P(C_A \mid H) = P(C_C \mid H) = \frac{1}{2}.$$

The scene on stage is exactly the same, yet the answer changes, because the **model** that produced the information changed. It is the same lesson as [Bertrand's paradox](../bertrand-paradox/index.qmd): to compute a probability, we need to know how the data came about.

The simulation below compares the two models and generalises to $n$ doors: the host opens $n - 2$ doors with goats and leaves one more door closed.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Simulation: n doors and two kinds of host
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof n26 = Inputs.range([3, 50], {label: "Doors", step: 1, value: 3})
viewof knows26 = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Knows where the car is", true], ["Opens doors at random", false]]), {label: "Host", value: true})
viewof go26 = Inputs.button("10,000 games")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  go26;
  let valid = 0, stayW = 0, switchW = 0;
  for (let g = 0; g < 10000; g++) {
    const car = Math.floor(n26 * Math.random()), pick = 0;
    let other;
    if (knows26) {
      // leaves the car door closed, or a random one if the car is behind our pick
      other = car !== pick ? car : 1 + Math.floor((n26 - 1) * Math.random());
    } else {
      // opens n − 2 random doors among the others, leaves one closed
      other = 1 + Math.floor((n26 - 1) * Math.random());
      if (car !== pick && car !== other) continue; // the car was revealed: the game is void
    }
    valid++;
    if (car === pick) stayW++; else switchW++;
  }
  const f = x => x.toLocaleString("en-GB", {style: "percent", minimumFractionDigits: 1, maximumFractionDigits: 1});
  const th = knows26 ? [1 / n26, (n26 - 1) / n26] : [0.5, 0.5];
  return html`<table class="ix-tbl">
    <tr><th></th><th>Stay</th><th>Switch</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Win frequency</td><td><b>${f(stayW / valid)}</b></td><td><b>${f(switchW / valid)}</b></td></tr>
    <tr><td>Exact value</td><td>${f(th[0])}</td><td>${f(th[1])}</td></tr></table>
    <div class="ix-note">Counted ${valid.toLocaleString("en-GB")} games${knows26 ? "" : html`. In the rest the host accidentally revealed the car and they were voided`}.
    ${knows26 ? html` With ${n26} doors switching wins with probability ${n26 - 1}/${n26}: the first pick "keeps" only 1/${n26}.` : html` Without knowledge, the goat that was revealed is just luck, and the two closed doors are equally likely.`}</div>`;
}
```
:::

With 50 doors switching becomes obvious: you picked one, the host opened 48 goats and left **one particular** door closed. The car is almost certainly there.

## The same in R

```{r}
#| label: monty-sim
play <- function(switch_door) {
  car <- sample(3, 1); pick <- sample(3, 1)
  goats <- setdiff(1:3, c(pick, car))
  opened <- if (length(goats) == 1) goats else sample(goats, 1)
  if (switch_door) pick <- setdiff(1:3, c(pick, opened))
  pick == car
}
c(stay = mean(replicate(20000, play(FALSE))), switch = mean(replicate(20000, play(TRUE))))
```

Note the line with `sample(goats, 1)`: when R's `sample()` gets a single number $k$, it samples from $1{:}k$. That is why we first check whether only one goat door is available. It is a classic trap in R simulations.

## Key takeaways

- If the host knows where the car is and always opens a goat door, **switching wins with probability 2/3**.
- Your first pick keeps probability $1/3$, because the host's action gives no information about it.
- If the host opens doors at random, the two closed doors are equally likely.
- The same observation yields different probabilities under different models: Bayes' likelihoods depend on how the data arose.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz26 = [
  {q: "With 10 doors, the host (who knows) opens 8 with goats. What is your chance of winning if you switch?",
   opts: ["1/2", "1/10", "9/10", "8/10"], ans: 2,
   why: "Your first door keeps 1/10. The remaining 9/10 goes to the only other closed door."},
  {q: "The host opens a door at random and happens to show a goat. What do you do?",
   opts: ["Switch: 2/3", "Stay: 2/3", "It does not matter: 1/2 each"], ans: 2,
   why: "Without knowledge, the goat was not 'chosen'. Bayes gives 1/2 to each closed door."},
  {q: "In the classic game, if you picked A, what is P(the host opens B | the car is behind C)?",
   opts: ["0", "1/2", "1", "1/3"], ans: 2,
   why: "He cannot open A (your pick) or C (the car), so he must open B."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz26.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz26.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** In the classic game, suppose that whenever the host can choose between two goat doors, he **always** opens B if he can. You picked A and he opened B. What is your chance of winning if you switch?

**3.** Modify `play()` for the version where the host opens a door at random, and confirm the probability $1/2$ by keeping only the games where he showed a goat.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. Now $P(H \mid C_A) = 1$ (he can choose and prefers B), $P(H \mid C_B) = 0$ and $P(H \mid C_C) = 1$. So $P(C_C \mid H) = \dfrac{1/3}{1/3 + 1/3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Switching never hurts, but here it does not help. Had the host opened C, however, you would know for sure that the car is behind B.
3. Replace the choice of `opened` with `opened <- sample(setdiff(1:3, pick), 1)`, return `NA` when `opened == car`, and compute `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)`.
:::
